 51% of Pre-Retirees Want to Semi-Retire. She Cut Her Schedule to Three Days, but Social Security Still Counts Her Pay
 Cutting to three days a week sounds like a clean workaround, but Social Security never looks at how many days you work, and that blind spot can freeze months of benefits you were counting on to replace those lost shifts.
 By Gerelyn Terzo 
 Published October 22, 2026, 5:30am ET · 4 min read 
 The Full Benefits Desk desk. Editor: Gerelyn Terzo .
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 51% of pre-retirees envision semi-retirement, but Social Security's earnings test measures total annual wages, not days worked.
 In 2026, earning above $24,480 triggers $1 withheld for every $2 earned, meaning a $45,000 part-time salary could cost $10,260 in benefits.
 Delaying Social Security filing avoids withheld checks and permanently boosts monthly benefits, making it the stronger choice when part-time pay covers expenses.

 A professional meticulously plans their weekly schedule, reflecting the careful adjustments many pre-retirees make when transitioning to a semi-retired work life while considering Social Security implications. © Woman using calendar app on computer in office ( Shutterstock.com ) by Kaspars Grinvalds 
 Picture a 63-year-old nurse who has worked five shifts a week for decades, then drops to three and files for Social Security, figuring part-time work won’t touch her checks. Plenty of people are drawing up the same plan. F&G Annuities & Life ( NYSE:FG | FG Price Prediction ), the annuity and life insurance company, found in a survey released earlier this month that 51% of surveyed pre-retirees imagine semi-retirement.
 On paper, the plan works: fewer days, a smaller paycheck, and a monthly Social Security deposit to fill the gap. The catch is that Social Security looks at what she earns over the year, and the number of days she works never enters the math.
 Social Security Counts Every Dollar You Earn
 Before full retirement age (FRA), Social Security applies a rule called the retirement earnings test . It adds up her wages from work for the year, and if they pass a set limit, some of the benefit gets held back. A three-day schedule and a five-day schedule are treated the same if the paychecks total the same amount.
 The Social Security Administration releases an annual fact sheet with the year’s benefit and tax figures. For 2026, it sets the limit for beneficiaries under full retirement age at $24,480 for the year. Above that line, Social Security withholds $1 for every $2 she earns.
 Only pay from work counts. Pension income, interest, dividends and withdrawals from retirement accounts don’t trigger any withholding.
 How $45,000 in Part-Time Pay Shrinks Her Checks
 Say her three days a week still bring in $45,000 for the year. That’s well over the limit, and $10,260 of her benefits could be withheld.
 Social Security generally collects that $10,260 by holding back whole monthly checks, then resumes payments once it has collected enough. If she was counting on those deposits to replace two lost shifts, months without a check could throw off her budget.
 Now picture her waiting instead. She keeps the reduced schedule, lets her wages cover the bills, and holds off on filing, so nothing gets withheld and every month she waits raises her eventual benefit for life. If she files early while earning well over the limit, she takes the permanent cut for claiming early and still goes months without a check.
 Withheld Months Earn Credit at FRA
 Withholding feels like a penalty, but it works differently from the cut for claiming early. When she reaches full retirement age, Social Security recalculates her benefit and credits every month her check was fully withheld. Those months are treated as if she never claimed them, so her monthly payment goes up from then on.
 The adjustment doesn’t completely erase the cost of claiming early. Social Security gives her credit for months she received no check, but the months she did collect early still leave her with a smaller benefit. The increase comes through future monthly checks, not a lump-sum refund.
 One more rule matters if she changes her schedule during the year she first claims. Social Security can pay a full check for any month she earns $2,040 or less in 2026, even if she earned more earlier in the year. But at $45,000 annually, her three-day schedule still works out to $3,750 a month, too much for that exception.
 Decide by Your Total Annual Paycheck
 Before filing, estimate her gross wages for the whole calendar year, including any overtime or bonuses on those three days. If the total lands well under $24,480, she can collect while semi-retired with nothing withheld. If it lands far above, as $45,000 does, the real question is whether her household budget works without the check.
 Filing early is the choice that’s toughest to undo, because that reduction lasts for life while withheld months eventually get credited back. If three days of pay already cover her bills, waiting usually means a bigger check later and no surprise gaps along the way. The earnings test is only one pitfall. Several tax traps catch people easing out of work in stages (we mapped out the other big ones in a free semi-retirement guide here ). A spouse’s benefits can change the logic. Health and savings can too, so it’s worth an hour with her own Social Security earnings record and a realistic pay estimate before she files.
